issues.subcategory: non-empirical dummy data used as results
issues.description: The manuscript explicitly states that the results are based on a randomized Qualtrics-generated dummy dataset, yet it presents inferential results and substantive conclusions as if they were empirical findings. Randomly generated data cannot provide evidence for or against the hypotheses, cannot estimate effect sizes, and cannot support claims about replication success or failure.
issues.quote: Results were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection.

issues.description: The manuscript alternates between saying that the methods/results are simulated and saying that data collection was completed before analyses. This creates a serious ambiguity about whether any actual data were collected, whether analyses are preregistered, and whether the results are real or placeholders.
issues.quote: Method and results sections were written using randomized dataset produced by Qualtrics to simulate what these sections will look like after data collection. These will be updated following the data collection. / All measures and manipulations conducted for this investigation are reported, and data collection was completed before analyses.

issues.description: The abstract reports null and positive findings based on the dummy dataset. Because the dataset was generated randomly for preregistration, p-values, effect sizes, confidence intervals, and hypothesis tests are meaningless and should not be interpreted as empirical support or non-support.
issues.quote: We generated a dummy set of samples in the Qualtrics survey (N = 1000) and found no empirical support for the effect of analytical reasoning on the identifiable victim effect. To extend the replication, we added the “perceived impact of donation” as a factor that is believed to be linked with the identifiable victim effect. Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.description: Participants are said to have selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions rather than being randomly assigned. This destroys the experimental basis for causal inference because condition differences may reflect pre-existing participant preferences, beliefs, motivation, or familiarity rather than the manipulation.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.description: The design is described as within-subject, but the cell sizes and analyses indicate a between-subjects 2 × 3 design with different participants in each cell. If the study was within-subject, the analysis should model repeated measures and order/carryover effects; if it was between-subjects, the design description is wrong. This is a fundamental design-reporting inconsistency.
issues.quote: We embedded Studies 1 and 3 of Small et al. (2007) into a single within-subject design with identifiability and intervention as the independent variables; donation and feeling variables as the dependent variables respectively.

issues.subcategory: wrong ANOVA model for stated design
issues.description: The authors report a standard two-way ANOVA, apparently treating observations as independent. That is inconsistent with the stated within-subject design; repeated-measures or mixed-effects models would be required if participants completed multiple conditions. The analysis model therefore may use the wrong error term and incorrect degrees of freedom.
issues.quote: We conducted a 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on donation.

issues.subcategory: combining distinct original studies changes design
issues.description: The replication merges two separate original experiments into one study and adds intervention conditions to the joint condition. This materially changes the experimental context, estimand, and participant experience, making it difficult to interpret the result as a close replication of either original Study 1 or Study 3.
issues.quote: In this replication, we merged Studies 1 and 3 into one single experiment to study both the explicit and implicit intervention of debiasing the identifiable victim effect, indicated in the imaginary donation to corresponding victims across conditions. The intervention of learning about the effect would also be applied to the joint condition to reveal a more comprehensive comparison between the explicit and implicit settings.

issues.subcategory: replication classified as close despite major deviations
issues.description: The manuscript classifies the study as a close-to-very-close replication despite acknowledging changes to the dependent variable, procedure, physical setting, context, sample, and incentive structure. These deviations are directly relevant to donation behavior and affective response, so the replication classification is overstated.
issues.quote: DV stimuli | Different | Question adjustment ... Imaginary donation Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter. ... Physical settings | Different | Online survey ... Contextual variables | Different | MTurk workers as participants ... Replication classification | close to very close replication

issues.description: The original outcome was actual donation of earned money, whereas the replication uses an imaginary donation. Hypothetical donation intentions are vulnerable to social desirability and hypothetical bias and may not validly measure actual charitable giving. This threatens construct validity and comparability with the target study.
issues.quote: Imaginary donation Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.description: The original design gave participants $5 before the donation decision; the replication explicitly removes that feature. Donating from an endowed amount differs psychologically from reporting a hypothetical amount, especially in endowment, house-money, and loss-aversion terms. This changes the dependent variable and decision context.
issues.quote: No reward acquired from a pre-survey  Participants will not conduct an irrelevant survey prior to the experiment to earn $5 for the donation

issues.description: The hypotheses refer to donations to an identifiable victim, but the replication asks for donations to the corresponding victim(s), which may differ across identifiable, statistical, and joint conditions. If the joint condition asks about donating to both the identifiable victim and statistical victims, it is not comparable to the original Study 3 outcome.
issues.quote: Participants are required to indicate how much they would donate from $0 to $5 to the corresponding victim(s) instead of donating the money to Save the Children after signing a charity request letter.

issues.description: The authors replace the original victim information with updated information from Save the Children but do not report any validation that the new stimuli are equivalent in vividness, severity, familiarity, affective content, or donation appeal. Changes in stimuli could account for differences from the original effect.
issues.quote: Updated victim information  We will present the participants with the most updated victim information retrieved from the website of Save the Children given that those used in the original study was dated two decades ago.

issues.description: The study is framed as testing deliberative or analytical thinking, but the manipulation is merely exposure to information about the identifiable victim effect or joint presentation of victim information. No manipulation check or direct measure verifies that participants engaged in deliberative, analytical, or calculative reasoning.
issues.quote: The research conducted by Small et al. (2007) showed that the identifiable victim effect could be eliminated by deliberative thinking, meaning that thinking analytically about your helping behaviour would reduce your motivation to offer assistance to a single beneficiary.

issues.subcategory: mislabeling joint presentation as implicit learning
issues.description: The manuscript labels the joint condition as 'implicitly learning' about the identifiable victim effect, even though participants are not actually taught the effect. Presenting statistics alongside an identifiable victim may induce comparison, dilution, or scope information, but it is not necessarily learning about the bias. This weakens the theoretical interpretation.
issues.quote: For Hypothesis 3 and 4, explicitly learning about the identifiable victim effect means that participants would be presented with prior research about the phenomenon while participants implicitly learning about the effect would not be presented with such information but with the provision of victim statistics in the identifiable victim condition.

issues.description: Perceived impact is defined as perceived efficacy of the donation, which is a cognitive appraisal, but the analysis treats it as a segregated affective reaction or feeling variable. This conflates conceptually distinct constructs and undermines interpretation of the affective-mechanism analyses.
issues.quote: Perceived impact refers to the perceived efficacy of contribution in expecting a favourable outcome (Erlandsson et al., 2015). / We conducted a  2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on segregated affective reactions ... Perceived impact (Extension)

issues.description: The manuscript combines upset, touched, sympathy, moral responsibility, donation appropriateness, and possibly perceived impact into an aggregated feeling score without reporting reliability, factor structure, scale justification, or whether these items should form a single construct. Aggregating heterogeneous cognitive, moral, and affective items can obscure or distort effects.
issues.quote: Identifiability and intervention on aggregated feelings  Note: combine segregated feelings into one aggregated feeling

issues.description: The manuscript does not provide the exact item wording, response scales, anchors, scoring rules, aggregation procedure, or reliability for the donation and feeling measures in the main text. Links to supplementary files are not a substitute for sufficient reporting needed to evaluate construct validity and reproducibility.
issues.quote: The session of “Procedure” in the supplementary summarizes the procedure of the current replication study. For the full reported survey, please access the Qualtrics survey with the link below

issues.description: The manuscript states that the study was powered but does not report the target power, alpha level, assumed effect size for each primary hypothesis, allocation ratio, exclusion inflation, or resulting required sample size in the main text. This prevents evaluation of whether the study is adequately powered, especially for interactions and added extension analyses.
issues.quote: To obtain the minimal sample size required for this study, The sample size for this study was determined to ensure adequate statistical power for detecting the effects reported in the original study. The full report of power analysis can be found in the supplementary under the section of “Power analysis of the original study effect”.

issues.description: Key sample characteristics needed to evaluate external validity and replication comparability are missing or inconsistent, including geographic origin and compensation. The table explicitly lists these as not specified, yet the design depends on an online MTurk sample and donation task where compensation is highly relevant.
issues.quote: Geographic origin | US American | Not specified | Not specified ... Compensation | US$5 | Not specified | Not specified

issues.description: The manuscript makes broad claims about human tendencies while the replication sample is an online MTurk sample with unspecified geographic origin and compensation. Without clear sampling information, the results cannot be generalized broadly to humans, donors, or charitable contexts.
issues.quote: The identifiable victim effect is the human’s tendency to offer greater support to an identifiable individual over a larger group of anonymous victims represented by numerical statistics (Jenni & Loewenstein, 1997). / Geographic origin | US American | Not specified | Not specified

issues.description: Participants with prior knowledge and failed attention checks are said to be excluded, but the manuscript does not report how many were excluded for each reason, whether exclusions were preregistered, whether exclusions differed by condition, or whether the final N reflects exclusions. The reported cell sizes sum exactly to 1000, creating ambiguity about whether exclusions occurred.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.description: The manuscript refers to excluding attention-check failures but does not report the attention-check item, timing, pass/fail rule, number excluded, or whether it could be affected by condition. This prevents evaluation of exclusion validity and replicability.
issues.quote: Participants who indicated they had prior knowledge of the identifiable victim effect were excluded, as well as those who failed the attention check.

issues.description: The manuscript does not describe how missing responses, partial completions, straight-lining, duplicate workers, or incomplete outcome data were handled. This is especially important for online MTurk/Qualtrics data, but no missing-data plan is reported in the main text.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration

issues.subcategory: ordinal bounded outcome analyzed without justification
issues.description: Donation is a bounded discrete $0–$5 response, and the original study reportedly used ordered probit regression. The replication drops ordered probit and relies on ANOVA/t tests without justification or robustness checks. Treating a six-point bounded response as normally distributed can affect inference, especially with unequal cell sizes or skewed donation distributions.
issues.quote: Ordered probit regression | a. effect of identifiability on donation ... This test would not be conducted in the replication

issues.description: The manuscript reports Cohen's d for Study 3 from a three-level omnibus ANOVA. An omnibus F with df1 = 2 does not map to a single Cohen's d without specifying a contrast; the appropriate omnibus effect would be eta-squared or Cohen's f. This affects power analysis and replication evaluation.
issues.quote: In Study 3, the effect of implicitly activating the analytical thinking mechanism on donation was d = 0.23, 95% CI [0.01, 0.45], regarded as a small effect.

issues.subcategory: replication effect not reported on same metric as original
issues.description: The planned replication evaluation compares the original effect size d = 0.48 with the replication effect, but the results table reports partial eta-squared for a modified 2 × 3 ANOVA rather than the same contrast and effect-size metric. This prevents valid application of the stated replication-evaluation criteria.
issues.quote: We aim to study the effect of deliberative thinking on identifiable victim effect by comparing the replication effect with the original effect (d = 0.48, 95% CI [0.11, 0.84])

issues.description: The authors interpret the main effect of identifiability even though the identifiability × intervention interaction is significant. Main effects averaged over interacting factors can be misleading; the interaction should be decomposed using simple effects or planned contrasts aligned with the hypotheses.
issues.quote: Results from Table 9 showed that no significant effect was found on intervention but the identifiability and the interaction effect of identifiability and intervention was supported. To further deduce the particular conditions in resulting the above significant findings, we performed post-hoc tests for the difference of identifiability on donation.

issues.subcategory: arbitrary contrast does not test interaction
issues.description: After finding an interaction, the authors compare the identifiable/no-intervention cell against the average of five heterogeneous conditions. This contrast collapses statistical, identifiable-intervention, joint-intervention, and joint-no-intervention conditions, does not isolate either the explicit-intervention effect or the implicit joint-condition effect, and differs from the original 2 × 2 contrast.
issues.quote: Given the significant interaction effect, we also conducted a t-test to study if the mean of  identifiable/no intervention condition is different from the mean of combining other five conditions on donation.

issues.description: The text reverses or mislabels the identifiable and statistical condition means. Table 7 implies that the identifiable condition has higher average donation than the statistical condition, but the results text states that statistical victims had M = 2.54 and identifiable victims had M = 2.24. This changes the direction of the reported identifiable-victim effect.
issues.quote: From Table 10, we noticed that there is a significant difference between identifiable and statistical victim condition, t(994)=-2.40, SE=0.13, p=.049, meaning that participants who faced a statistical victim (M=2.54, SD=1.76) tended to donate more than those who faced the identifiable victims (M=2.24, SD=1.67).

issues.subcategory: test statistic sign inconsistent with interpretation
issues.description: For the identifiable versus statistical comparison, the reported t statistic is negative while the reported Cohen's d is positive and the condition means are inconsistently described. This suggests either contrast coding, sign, or labeling errors in the post-hoc output and makes the direction of the effect unclear.

The reported Cohen's d values for post-hoc contrasts appear inconsistent with the t statistics and mean differences. For example, t = 2.40 with large independent groups would imply a larger standardized mean difference than d = 0.076. This suggests incorrect effect-size computation or reporting.

issues.subcategory: confidence intervals inconsistent with significant p-values
issues.description: The post-hoc tables report significant Bonferroni-adjusted p-values while the associated 95% confidence intervals include zero. For a correctly matched two-sided confidence interval for the tested contrast, significance at p < .05 should generally correspond to a CI excluding zero. This indicates that the CIs may refer to a different statistic, are miscomputed, or are mislabeled.

The abstract claims support for lower perceived impact for identifiable victims and joint victims, but the reported post-hoc tests show only a significant statistical-victim versus joint-condition comparison; identifiable versus statistical is non-significant. The stated conclusion is therefore not supported by the reported tests.
issues.quote: Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics. / Identifiable VS Statistical | 994 | 0.91 | 0.11 | 0.03 | [-0.12,0.18] | 1.000

issues.description: The extension hypothesis predicts higher perceived impact for identifiable victims than statistical victims, but the abstract reports the opposite direction. This internal contradiction makes it unclear what the extension was intended to test and whether interpretation was driven by the observed dummy-data pattern.
issues.quote: 6 (Extension) | An identifiable victim elicits higher perceived impact of donation than statistical victims / Results have supported the hypothesis that people have a lower rating of perceived impact of donation when they faced an identifiable victim or an identifiable victim provided with victim statistics.

issues.description: The study conducts many tests across donation, aggregated feelings, six segregated feelings, interactions, post-hoc comparisons, and six correlations. Apart from selected Bonferroni pairwise tests, there is no correction or error-rate plan for the overall family of tests, increasing the risk of false-positive findings such as the p = .045 perceived-impact result.
issues.quote: Table 13 Summary of statistical tests for segregated feelings ... Upsetting ... Sympathy ... Touched ... Moral responsibility ... Donation appropriateness ... Perceived impact (Extension)

issues.description: The analysis plan uses conditional testing rules, conducting some tests only if earlier tests are significant. Such data-dependent branching can inflate researcher degrees of freedom unless fully preregistered with clear decision rules and familywise error control.
issues.quote: Post-hoc contrast test   (Note: we conduct the test only if the interaction effect is significant)

issues.subcategory: unclear primary outcome and primary test
issues.description: The manuscript lists multiple hypotheses and many analyses but does not clearly identify a single primary replication test, primary estimand, or hierarchy among donation, aggregate feelings, segregated feelings, perceived impact, and correlations. This ambiguity complicates interpretation of replication success and increases analytic flexibility.
issues.quote: Table 5 compares the statistical tests adopted in the original study and replication.

issues.description: The manuscript uses cross-sectional correlations between feelings and donation to examine whether feelings 'predict' donation, but the feelings were measured after donation in the original procedure and are not experimentally manipulated. These analyses cannot establish temporal prediction or causal influence of affective feelings on giving.
issues.quote: After the donation, they had to fill up a questionnaire for different cognitive evaluations they experienced which may influence their choice of donation. / We conducted a correlation between aggregated feelings and donation to examine whether affective feelings predict donation.

issues.description: The stated goal is to examine the effect of affective feelings on the identifiable victim effect, but the design does not manipulate affective feelings or conduct a valid mediation analysis. Correlations between post-decision feelings and donations cannot identify the affective mechanism.
issues.quote: The second goal of the current research is to examine the effect of affective feelings on the studied phenomenon, with the introduction of an extension known as the perceived impact of donation.

issues.subcategory: demand characteristics from explicit bias instruction
issues.description: Teaching participants about the identifiable victim effect immediately before a donation decision may create demand characteristics: participants may infer the desired response and change donations to appear unbiased rather than because of deliberative reasoning. The manuscript does not report procedures to assess or mitigate demand.
issues.quote: In Study 1 of Small et al. (2007), participants under manipulation were taught about the identifiable victim effect before donating to the victims.

issues.description: The methods do not describe any randomization algorithm, allocation concealment, balancing, or blocking. This is especially problematic because the procedure says participants selected their conditions, contradicting experimental assignment.
issues.quote: Participants selected their preferred intervention and identifiability conditions.

issues.subcategory: online setting changes control over procedure
issues.description: Moving from an in-person laboratory/student-center donation task to an online Qualtrics/MTurk survey reduces control over attention, environment, comprehension, and perceived reality of the donation. The manuscript acknowledges the change but does not describe compensatory controls beyond an unspecified attention check.
issues.quote: Online survey Participants will conduct an online survey in Qualtrics on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study surveyed inside a student center of a university in Pennsylvania

issues.description: For an MTurk sample, the manuscript does not report worker qualifications, location restrictions, approval rate thresholds, duplicate prevention, bot/VPN screening, IP/geolocation checks, or exclusion rules for low-quality responses. These are necessary for evaluating online data quality.
issues.quote: MTurk workers as participants We will recruit participants on the Mechanical Amazon Turk platform while the original study recruited participants sitting inside the school centre of a university in Pennsylvania

issues.subcategory: software versions and reproducibility details missing
issues.description: The analysis software is named, but versions, packages/functions, model specifications, contrast coding, and exact R code used for confidence intervals are not reported in the manuscript. This limits reproducibility, especially given inconsistencies in reported statistics.
issues.quote: We conducted the data analysis with JAMOVI for statistical testing and R for calculation of 95%CI given that such function is not available for ANOVA testing in JAMOVI.

issues.subcategory: factor definition of identifiability confounded by joint condition
issues.description: The identifiability factor has levels 'identifiable,' 'statistical,' and 'joint.' The joint condition differs not only in identifiability but also in amount/type of information and comparison context. Treating this as a simple main effect of identifiability confounds identifiability with information structure.
issues.quote: We conducted a 2 (intervention) X 3 (identifiability) two way ANOVA to examine the effect of identifiability and intervention on donation.

issues.subcategory: intervention factor confounded across original studies
issues.description: The intervention factor combines explicit teaching about the bias with the implicit joint-presentation manipulation. These are conceptually different manipulations, yet the merged 2 × 3 design treats them under a common intervention framework. This makes interpretation of intervention main effects and interactions unclear.
issues.quote: We merged Studies 1 and 3 into one single experiment to study both the explicit and implicit intervention of debiasing the identifiable victim effect

issues.subcategory: sample table contains duplicated replication columns
issues.description: Table 4 appears to contain duplicate columns for the replication sample, both labeled with the same Qualtrics-generated response information. This suggests table-formatting or reporting errors and makes the sample comparison difficult to interpret.
issues.quote: Table 4  Difference and similarities between the original study and replication ... Sample size | Study 1: 121 Study 3: 159 | 1000 | 1000

issues.subcategory: unrealistic generated demographics treated as participant data
issues.description: The demographics are reported as if they describe participants, but they come from Qualtrics-generated dummy responses and include an implausibly wide age range. Treating simulated demographics as sample characteristics is misleading.
issues.quote: A total of 1000 responses were generated from the Qualtrics for pre-registration (Mage = 67.80, SD=30.10; 471 females and 529 males).

issues.subcategory: external supplementary reliance with incomplete links
issues.description: Several key materials are said to be in external cloud folders, and some links are placeholders. Reliance on non-archival or incomplete links threatens long-term reproducibility and prevents full evaluation from the manuscript alone.
issues.quote: Cloud folder for presentation (PPT and PDF) | <enter link here> / Cloud folder for peer reviews | <enter link here>

issues.description: The manuscript attributes the identifiable victim effect to the availability heuristic, but the described mechanism is primarily affective vividness and sympathy rather than ease of memory retrieval. This risks conflating availability, affect heuristic, identifiability, and vividness mechanisms without clear predictions separating them.
issues.quote: Another reason to explain the identifiable victim effect is attributed to different psychological reasoning mechanisms in making judgments. The “availability heuristic”  (Tversky & Kahneman, 1973), which relies on the ease of retrieving relevant instances from memory, is believed to be activated when we value a personalized individual (Small & Loewenstein, 2003).

issues.description: The study concerns a specific charity-style appeal about starvation/Africa/Save the Children, but the introduction and discussion-like framing imply broader conclusions about prosocial behavior, resource allocation, and moral judgment. The manuscript does not sufficiently limit claims to this charitable-donation context.
issues.quote: The inconsistent prosocial motivation not only demonstrates human sense of unfairness in valuing life, but also highlights the lack of efficiency in resource allocation when asserts are accumulated on a single victim instead of dispersing to a greater population to benefit the society as a whole.
